subtopic_detail: Drooling and refusal to drink in a toddler forty five minutes after swallowing strongly alkaline dishwasher powder
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a two year old boy who was found by his grandmother next to an open dishwasher with white powder around his mouth about forty five minutes ago. The container confirms a strongly alkaline detergent powder.

He vomited once on the way in and has since been dribbling saliva continuously down his chin and turning his head away from the cup of water offered to him. His voice sounds normal when he cries and his grandmother has already spoken to the Poisons Information Centre.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Continuous drooling with pooling of saliva, patchy erythema of the tongue and soft palate with a white plaque on the left buccal mucosa, no stridor and no hoarseness, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft and not tender, no subcutaneous emphysema in the neck

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Keep him nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and arrange upper gastrointestinal endoscopy within the next twelve to twenty four hours
options.rationale: Drooling, vomiting and refusal to drink after an alkaline ingestion together predict significant oesophageal injury, and endoscopy between twelve and twenty four hours grades that injury when the burn has declared itself but before the tissue is at its most friable. Grading determines feeding, stricture surveillance and prognosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology

options.text: Give a single dose of activated charcoal by mouth to limit further absorption and observe him in the department for four hours
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind corrosives, obscures the mucosal view at endoscopy and risks a devastating aspiration into an already injured airway. It is reserved for ingestions of adsorbable toxins presenting within an hour with a protected airway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology

options.text: Encourage him to drink milk or water to dilute the alkali remaining in the oesophagus and observe him in the department overnight
options.rationale: Dilution has no proven benefit beyond the first few minutes and provokes vomiting, which re exposes the oesophagus to the corrosive on the way back up. Small volumes of water may be offered immediately after ingestion, not forty five minutes later in a child who is drooling. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

options.text: Give a weak acidic drink such as diluted lemon juice to neutralise the alkali and reassess his ability to swallow after one hour
options.rationale: Neutralisation is an exothermic reaction that adds a thermal burn to a chemical one, and it has no place in modern management. This is the classic anti pattern that the history of corrosive injury was written to abolish. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

options.text: Commence high dose oral corticosteroids immediately to prevent later oesophageal stricture formation and review him in clinic in a week
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have never been shown to prevent stricture after corrosive injury and they mask the fever and peritonism that signal perforation. Their limited remaining role is decided by the endoscopic grade in specialist hands, not empirically before the oesophagus has been seen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology

explanation.summary: Alkaline corrosives cause liquefactive necrosis, which penetrates deeply and continues to injure tissue after contact, whereas acids cause coagulative necrosis that tends to be more superficial in the oesophagus. Dishwasher and laundry detergents are among the commonest strongly alkaline agents in Australian homes and account for a large share of paediatric corrosive exposures. The presence of oral burns is an unreliable guide to what lies below, since serious oesophageal injury occurs with a normal mouth and an inflamed mouth may sit above a normal oesophagus, so the clinical triad of drooling, vomiting and dysphagia is used instead to select children for endoscopy. Timing matters because endoscopy before twelve hours may underestimate a burn that has not yet declared itself, while after about forty eight hours the wall is maximally friable and perforation risk rises. Long term, the concerns are stricture formation over subsequent weeks and a lifelong increase in oesophageal carcinoma risk.
key_points: Alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis that penetrates deeply and keeps injuring after contact.
Oral burns neither confirm nor exclude oesophageal injury.
Drooling, vomiting and refusal to drink together predict significant injury and select for endoscopy.
Charcoal, induced emesis, dilution beyond the first minutes and neutralisation are all contraindicated.
Endoscopy at twelve to twenty four hours grades the burn and guides feeding and stricture follow up.
explanation.pearls: Stridor, hoarseness or drooling with respiratory distress after a corrosive ingestion mandates airway assessment by an anaesthetist before anything else, because supraglottic oedema can progress over hours and a delayed intubation in a swollen corrosive injured airway is extremely difficult.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Corrosive ingestion

subtopic_detail: Profuse purulent discharge from both eyes with marked lid swelling on the third day of life after an unbooked pregnancy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the postnatal ward to see a baby girl on her third day of life. The midwife reports that both eyes began weeping yesterday evening and that this morning there is thick yellow discharge that reaccumulates within minutes of being wiped away.

Her mother arrived in labour without any antenatal care and no antenatal screening bloods or swabs were taken. The baby is feeding, has a normal temperature and has passed urine and meconium normally.

data_table.Examination: Marked bilateral eyelid oedema requiring gentle retraction to open the lids, profuse purulent discharge reaccumulating immediately, intense conjunctival injection and chemosis, corneas appear clear on the limited view obtained, no vesicles on the lids or scalp, anterior fontanelle soft, tone normal, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing, give parenteral ceftriaxone and start hourly saline eye irrigation
options.rationale: Hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis with marked lid oedema in the first five days is gonococcal until proven otherwise, and it perforates the cornea within twenty four to forty eight hours if untreated. Parenteral third generation cephalosporin with frequent saline irrigation and urgent ophthalmology review is the standard Australian response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing and commence topical chloramphenicol drops two hourly to both eyes
options.rationale: Topical therapy alone does not clear gonococcal infection and does not treat the concurrent mucosal colonisation of the nasopharynx and rectum that drives relapse. Topical treatment is adequate for the non gonococcal bacterial conjunctivitis that presents later and without this degree of lid oedema. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing and commence a two week course of oral erythromycin for the baby
options.rationale: Oral erythromycin treats neonatal chlamydial infection, which is the near pair here, but chlamydia characteristically appears between the fifth and fourteenth days with a less purulent discharge and far less lid swelling. Chlamydia also needs treating if the testing confirms it, but it is not the organism that threatens this cornea today. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Gonorrhoea)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Gonorrhoea

options.text: Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing and observe with regular saline cleaning and review the eyes tomorrow
options.rationale: Observation is appropriate for the sticky eye of nasolacrimal duct obstruction, where the conjunctiva stays white and the lids are not swollen. Applying it to a hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis risks corneal perforation and permanent blindness within a day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Take conjunctival swabs for viral testing and commence intravenous aciclovir with topical antiviral therapy to both affected eyes
options.rationale: Neonatal herpes simplex can involve the eye but produces a serous rather than frankly purulent discharge, usually with skin vesicles or dendritic corneal ulceration. Aciclovir becomes the priority if vesicles appear or if the baby develops encephalopathy or hepatitis. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Gonorrhoea)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Gonorrhoea

explanation.summary: Ophthalmia neonatorum means conjunctivitis in the first month of life, and the organism is predicted with reasonable accuracy by the day of onset and the character of the discharge. Neisseria gonorrhoeae presents between day one and day five with hyperacute profuse pus and dramatic lid oedema, and is the only cause that penetrates an intact corneal epithelium, which is why it can perforate the globe within two days. Chlamydia trachomatis is commoner overall but appears from day five to fourteen with a mucopurulent discharge and threatens the lungs rather than the cornea. The absence of antenatal screening is the single most important risk factor in this vignette, since Australian antenatal care would ordinarily have detected and treated maternal infection. Both mother and her sexual partners require testing and treatment, and both infections are notifiable.
key_points: Onset on days one to five with profuse pus and lid oedema indicates gonococcal infection.
Gonococcus can penetrate intact corneal epithelium and perforate the globe within forty eight hours.
Chlamydial ophthalmia presents from day five to fourteen and is treated with oral erythromycin.
Parenteral cephalosporin plus frequent saline irrigation is required, not topical therapy alone.
Test and treat the mother and her partners, and notify both infections.
explanation.pearls: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis requires oral rather than topical treatment because around half of affected infants are also colonised in the nasopharynx and go on to develop an afebrile staccato cough pneumonitis between four and twelve weeks of age.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Gonorrhoea

subtopic_detail: Displaced elbow fracture in a school aged child whose hand stays warm and pink with no palpable radial pulse
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar caring for a six year old boy who fell from the monkey bars onto an outstretched hand an hour ago. There is an obvious deformity just above the elbow and he is in considerable pain despite intranasal fentanyl.

Radiographs show a completely displaced extension type supracondylar humeral fracture with no cortical contact. The orthopaedic registrar is currently in theatre with another case and asks you for your assessment over the phone.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Gross swelling and an S shaped deformity above the elbow with intact skin, hand warm with capillary refill of two seconds and pink nail beds, radial pulse not palpable and not detectable on handheld Doppler, forearm compartments soft and not tense, cannot make the circle sign with thumb and index finger, sensation intact over all digits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange immediate transfer to theatre for urgent closed reduction and percutaneous wire fixation with reassessment of the limb afterwards
options.rationale: In a completely displaced supracondylar fracture the brachial artery is usually tented or kinked by the proximal fragment rather than transected, so reduction itself is the vascular intervention and it must not wait. The inability to make the circle sign indicates an anterior interosseous nerve palsy, which is a further indication for urgent operative reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus

options.text: Apply an above elbow backslab in thirty degrees of flexion and arrange review in the fracture clinic within the next forty eight hours
options.rationale: Outpatient management is appropriate for undisplaced fractures with cortical contact, not for a completely displaced fracture with an absent pulse and a nerve deficit. Delaying reduction here allows progressive swelling that makes both reduction and vascular recovery harder. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus

options.text: Request an urgent computed tomography angiogram of the affected limb to define the arterial anatomy before any reduction is attempted
options.rationale: Angiography delays the reduction that usually restores flow and rarely alters the operative plan, since the injury site is already known from the fracture. It has a role only if the hand remains poorly perfused after a satisfactory reduction. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus

options.text: Refer him directly to the vascular surgery service for exploration of the brachial artery before any manipulation of the fracture is performed
options.rationale: Exploration before reduction operates on an artery whose problem is mechanical displacement, and most such arteries are found kinked rather than divided. Vascular involvement is warranted when the hand remains white and pulseless after the fracture has been reduced and stabilised. (Source: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus

options.text: Perform a closed reduction under procedural sedation in the emergency department and apply a plaster backslab once the alignment looks acceptable
options.rationale: A completely displaced supracondylar fracture is inherently unstable and redisplaces in plaster, so reduction without wire fixation fails and risks a cubitus varus deformity. Emergency department reduction is appropriate only as an emergency manoeuvre for a critically ischaemic limb when theatre is genuinely unavailable. (Source: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric supracondylar fractures)
source_refs: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric supracondylar fractures

explanation.summary: Supracondylar humeral fracture is the commonest elbow fracture of childhood and peaks between five and seven years, almost always from a fall onto an outstretched hand producing an extension type injury. The proximal fragment displaces anteriorly into the antecubital fossa, where it threatens the brachial artery and the median nerve with its anterior interosseous branch. The pink pulseless hand is the classic dilemma: perfusion is maintained by collateral flow around the elbow, and because the artery is usually kinked rather than cut, prompt reduction and stabilisation restores the pulse in most children. Anterior interosseous nerve injury produces weakness of the flexor pollicis longus and the index flexor digitorum profundus, so the child cannot make an O shape with thumb and index finger, and it recovers spontaneously in the great majority over weeks to months. A genuinely white pulseless hand is a surgical emergency of a different order and goes straight to theatre with vascular surgery on standby.
key_points: Extension type displacement drives the proximal fragment towards the brachial artery and median nerve.
A pink pulseless hand reflects collateral perfusion and is treated by urgent reduction and fixation.
Inability to make the circle sign indicates anterior interosseous nerve palsy.
Angiography and vascular exploration are reserved for persistent ischaemia after reduction.
Completely displaced fractures need percutaneous wires because plaster alone allows redisplacement.
explanation.pearls: Document the anterior interosseous nerve with the circle sign specifically, because it is a pure motor nerve with no sensory territory and a palsy present before reduction is entirely missed unless thumb interphalangeal and index distal interphalangeal flexion are tested individually.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric supracondylar fractures
BMJ Best Practice: Supracondylar humeral fracture

subtopic_detail: Six months of pain around the navel in a thriving nine year old with normal screening bloods whose parents want a scan
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a nine year old girl referred with six months of tummy pain. Her mother describes it as being around the belly button, coming on most school mornings, lasting an hour or two and easing at weekends and during the holidays.

She has never woken from sleep with the pain. Her growth has tracked the 50th centile for height and weight throughout, she has missed eleven days of school this term, and her parents have asked specifically for a scan because they are worried something is being missed.

data_table.Examination: Growth on the 50th centile for height and weight with no fall off, abdomen soft with mild periumbilical tenderness and no guarding, no mass or organomegaly, perianal inspection normal, no mouth ulcers, no clubbing, no rash, no joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), albumin 41 g/L (35 to 50), coeliac serology negative with a normal total immunoglobulin A, faecal calprotectin 22 micrograms/g (less than 50), urine microscopy and culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound to complete the assessment and reassure the family that no structural abnormality is present
options.rationale: Ultrasound in a thriving child with normal screening tests has a very low yield and frequently turns up incidental findings that generate further anxiety and further tests. Imaging is indicated for a palpable mass, organomegaly, or pain with vomiting or urinary symptoms. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain

options.text: Make and explain a positive diagnosis of functional abdominal pain and agree a graded return to school plan with planned review
options.rationale: Functional abdominal pain is diagnosed positively on a characteristic history with normal growth, a normal examination and no alarm features, not by exhausting investigations. Naming the diagnosis, explaining gut and brain signalling and restoring school attendance are the interventions that actually change the outcome. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain

options.text: Refer her for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsies to look for an inflammatory or coeliac cause of the pain
options.rationale: Endoscopy under general anaesthetic cannot be justified with negative coeliac serology, a normal calprotectin and no weight loss or bleeding. It becomes appropriate when there is dysphagia, haematemesis, persistent vomiting or unexplained weight loss. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain

options.text: Commence a trial of a proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks and review whether the frequency of her morning pain has improved
options.rationale: Acid suppression has no role in periumbilical pain without heartburn or epigastric burning, and prescribing it medicalises the problem while implying an organic disease that has not been found. A trial would be reasonable for genuine dyspeptic symptoms localised to the epigastrium. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain

options.text: Advise a strict exclusion diet removing lactose and wheat for six weeks and review whether the pattern of her symptoms changes
options.rationale: Broad exclusion diets in children risk nutritional inadequacy and entrench illness behaviour around food, and the evidence for them in functional pain is weak. Any dietary manipulation should be short, targeted and dietitian supervised rather than open ended self imposed restriction. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Functional gastrointestinal disorders)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Functional gastrointestinal disorders

explanation.summary: Functional abdominal pain affects up to one in ten school aged children and is the commonest cause of recurrent abdominal pain in this age group. It is a positive diagnosis resting on a typical history, normal growth, a normal examination and the absence of alarm features such as weight loss, nocturnal waking with pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, unexplained fever or a family history of inflammatory bowel disease. Pain that is worse on school days and absent in holidays points strongly to a functional disorder with a school related trigger, and school avoidance is often the most disabling consequence rather than the pain itself. Continuing to investigate a child who meets these criteria reinforces the family's belief that a serious disease is being missed and makes the pain harder to treat. Management combines explanation of the gut and brain axis, restoration of normal function, and psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy or gut directed hypnotherapy where symptoms persist.
key_points: Functional abdominal pain is diagnosed positively, not by exclusion after exhaustive testing.
Normal growth with a normal examination and normal screening tests is highly reassuring.
Alarm features include weight loss, nocturnal pain, bleeding, vomiting and a family history of inflammatory bowel disease.
Symptoms worse on school days and absent in holidays suggest a school related trigger.
Cognitive behavioural therapy and gut directed hypnotherapy have the best evidence for persistent symptoms.
explanation.pearls: A faecal calprotectin below 50 micrograms per gram has a negative predictive value above 95 per cent for paediatric inflammatory bowel disease, which is why a normal result in a thriving child without bleeding makes endoscopy very hard to justify.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Recurrent abdominal pain
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Functional gastrointestinal disorders
NICE: Coeliac disease recognition and assessment

subtopic_detail: Eight weeks of daily rattly cough in a thriving preschooler with a clear chest and a normal chest radiograph
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a four year old boy referred by his general practitioner with eight weeks of daily cough. His mother describes it as rattly and chesty, as though there is fluid in there, and says it happens throughout the day rather than only at night.

He has had two courses of oral salbutamol and a four week trial of an inhaled corticosteroid with no change at all in the cough. He attends kindergarten, his weight is on the 75th centile, and there was no episode of choking before the cough began.

data_table.Examination: Wet sounding cough audible in the room, chest clear on auscultation with no wheeze or crackles, no digital clubbing, no chest wall deformity, nasal mucosa normal with no purulent postnasal discharge, tympanic membranes normal, growth on the 75th centile
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph reported as normal with clear lung fields and no bronchial wall thickening, sweat chloride 18 mmol/L (less than 30), immunoglobulins within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a two to four week course of oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review whether the cough has completely resolved
options.rationale: A wet cough lasting longer than four weeks in a thriving child with a normal examination and radiograph, unresponsive to bronchodilator and inhaled steroid, defines protracted bacterial bronchitis, and the diagnosis is confirmed by resolution on a prolonged course of amoxicillin with clavulanate. Treating it properly matters because repeated untreated episodes progress to bronchiectasis. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children

options.text: Increase the dose of the inhaled corticosteroid and add a long acting beta agonist, then reassess his response in four weeks
options.rationale: Asthma produces a dry cough with wheeze and variability, and this child has a consistently wet cough that has already failed both a bronchodilator and four weeks of inhaled steroid. Escalating asthma therapy in a child who has not responded to it is a common and harmful anti pattern. (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook)
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook

options.text: Arrange a high resolution computed tomography scan of the chest to look for early bronchiectasis before starting any further treatment
options.rationale: Computed tomography delivers a significant radiation dose and is not the first step when a therapeutic trial will both treat and diagnose the commonest cause. It is indicated when the wet cough fails to resolve after two adequate antibiotic courses or recurs repeatedly. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children

options.text: Refer him for flexible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage to obtain airway samples and exclude an inhaled foreign body
options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is invasive and requires general anaesthesia, and there was no choking episode and no focal radiographic or auscultatory finding to suggest a retained foreign body. It is reserved for treatment failure, recurrent episodes or a genuine suspicion of an airway lesion. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children

options.text: Reassure his mother that the cough is a post viral phenomenon in a kindergarten child and review him again in a further eight weeks
options.rationale: Post viral cough is dry and settles within three to four weeks, whereas a wet cough persisting beyond four weeks is abnormal and demands an explanation. Watchful waiting here allows a treatable neutrophilic airway infection to continue damaging the airway wall. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children

explanation.summary: Protracted bacterial bronchitis is the commonest cause of chronic wet cough in Australian preschool children and results from persistent neutrophilic airway infection, typically with non typeable Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae or Moraxella catarrhalis, growing within a biofilm on the airway wall. The defining triad is a wet cough of more than four weeks, absence of any pointer to an alternative diagnosis, and resolution on an appropriate antibiotic course. The character of the cough is the most useful single discriminator, because asthma and post viral cough are dry while protracted bacterial bronchitis is consistently wet, and this explains the complete failure of asthma therapy in such children. Two weeks of amoxicillin with clavulanate resolves the cough in most, with a further two weeks for those who do not respond fully. This matters because recurrent or inadequately treated episodes sit on a continuum that leads through chronic suppurative lung disease to established bronchiectasis, a pathway of particular importance in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children.
key_points: A wet cough beyond four weeks in a child is never normal and needs a diagnosis.
Failure to respond to bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids argues strongly against asthma.
Protracted bacterial bronchitis is confirmed by resolution on two to four weeks of amoxicillin with clavulanate.
Normal growth, clear chest and normal radiograph do not exclude the diagnosis.
Recurrent untreated episodes progress towards chronic suppurative lung disease and bronchiectasis.
explanation.pearls: Refer for bronchoscopy and high resolution computed tomography if a child needs more than two courses of antibiotics in twelve months for wet cough, because recurrent protracted bacterial bronchitis at that frequency carries a substantial risk of established bronchiectasis on imaging.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic wet cough in children
National Asthma Council Australia: Australian Asthma Handbook
BMJ Best Practice: Chronic cough in children

subtopic_detail: Toddler treated as gastroenteritis who has an enlarged liver and a gallop and deteriorates after an initial fluid bolus
stem:
You are the sole doctor on an evening shift in a regional emergency department caring for a three year old girl referred with two days of vomiting and poor oral intake. She was treated as gastroenteritis by her general practitioner this morning.

On arrival she was mottled and listless with cool hands and feet, so you gave 10 mL/kg of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent over fifteen minutes. Her mother says there has been no diarrhoea at all and that her breathing has become faster since she arrived. The nearest paediatric intensive care unit is four hours away by road.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 186 beats per minute, blood pressure 78/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent in room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Liver edge palpable 4 cm below the costal margin, added third heart sound audible at the apex, fine crackles at both lung bases that were not present on arrival, capillary refill 4 seconds peripherally, no rash, no neck stiffness, abdomen otherwise soft with no tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph showing an enlarged cardiac silhouette with upper lobe venous distension, electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia with low voltage QRS complexes and T wave inversion in the lateral leads, venous lactate 4.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0), sodium 136 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), glucose 5.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Give a further 20 mL/kg bolus of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent over ten minutes and reassess her perfusion and conscious state afterwards
options.rationale: Repeated rapid boluses are correct for septic or hypovolaemic shock but are actively harmful when the shock is cardiogenic, because a failing ventricle sits on the descending limb of the Starling curve and further preload worsens pulmonary oedema. The crackles and hepatomegaly that appeared after the first bolus are the warning that this pathway is wrong. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Myocarditis

options.text: Withhold further fluid boluses, arrange urgent echocardiography and contact the paediatric retrieval service to start inotropic support
options.rationale: Hepatomegaly, a gallop rhythm, new basal crackles and cardiomegaly with low voltage complexes identify cardiogenic shock from acute myocarditis, in which the priority is to stop giving volume and start careful inotropic support with expert retrieval advice. Any further fluid must be given in small aliquots of no more than 5 to 10 mL/kg with reassessment after each. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Myocarditis

options.text: Take blood cultures and give intravenous ceftriaxone with fluid resuscitation continued to a total of 60 mL/kg as per the sepsis pathway
options.rationale: The paediatric sepsis pathway is the correct default for an undifferentiated shocked child, and covering for sepsis remains reasonable, but driving the fluid component to 60 mL/kg in the face of clear cardiac failure will cause pulmonary oedema. The sepsis pathway itself directs clinicians to reassess for cardiac dysfunction after each bolus for precisely this reason. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin now at the dose used for Kawasaki disease and arrange transfer to the regional paediatric ward for observation
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is sometimes used in fulminant paediatric myocarditis but the evidence is weak and it does nothing for the immediate haemodynamic emergency in front of you. It is a decision for the receiving intensive care team after echocardiography, not a substitute for circulatory support and retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Myocarditis

options.text: Perform rapid sequence intubation now to reduce her work of breathing and then continue volume resuscitation once the airway is secured
options.rationale: Induction agents and positive pressure ventilation abolish sympathetic drive and reduce preload, and intubating a child in uncorrected cardiogenic shock without inotropic support first frequently precipitates arrest. If intubation becomes necessary it should follow the commencement of inotropes and be performed by the most experienced operator available. (Source: RCH CPG: Myocarditis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Myocarditis

explanation.summary: Acute myocarditis in young children is usually viral and characteristically masquerades as gastroenteritis, respiratory infection or sepsis, because vomiting, lethargy and poor feeding are its commonest presenting complaints and chest pain is rare below school age. The features that betray it are hepatomegaly, a gallop rhythm and respiratory signs that worsen rather than improve after fluid, together with cardiomegaly on the chest radiograph and low voltage complexes with repolarisation change on the electrocardiogram. Recognising this matters enormously because the standard shock response of repeated 20 mL/kg boluses is precisely the wrong treatment and can precipitate fulminant decompensation. Management is small cautious fluid aliquots if any, early inotropic support, avoidance of intubation until the circulation is supported, and urgent involvement of a paediatric retrieval service, since mechanical circulatory support may ultimately be required. Outcomes in children who survive the acute phase are surprisingly good, with many recovering normal ventricular function.
key_points: Vomiting and lethargy without diarrhoea should raise doubt about a diagnosis of gastroenteritis.
Hepatomegaly with a gallop rhythm and new basal crackles indicates cardiogenic rather than septic shock.
Low voltage complexes with cardiomegaly on the radiograph support acute myocarditis.
Fluid boluses beyond 5 to 10 mL/kg aliquots worsen cardiogenic shock and must be withheld.
Start inotropes and involve paediatric retrieval before contemplating intubation.
explanation.pearls: Palpate for the liver edge in every shocked child before the second fluid bolus, because a liver more than 2 cm below the costal margin in a toddler is the earliest and most reliable bedside sign that the shock is cardiogenic and that further volume will make things worse.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis assessment and management
BMJ Best Practice: Myocarditis in children
